The Middle East conflict has added to inflation risks and weighed on the growth outlook, while government bond yields have risen sharply. The UK 10-year gilt yield is now at the top of t he G7 range (Figure 2), meaning any additional borrowing comes at a high cost. This matters because even relatively small changes in expected growth, inflation or interest costs can m eaningfully reduce the Chancellor’s margin against the fiscal rules. This leaves a difficult balance for the Budget. The government has committed to maintaining the existing fiscal framework, but also faces pressure to support growth, ease the burden on households and businesses, and respond to a less favourable global environment. records.text: berg Despite the above -mentioned risks, GBP options are not pricing an unusually disruptive fiscal event. Based on the excess variance of two-week over one-week GBPUSD ATM volatility measured 10 business days before the Budget, we estimate the option -implied Budget -day move at around 0.28%. This compares with an average implied premium of 0.47% ahead of the previous five fiscal events and an average realised Budget -day move of 0.40% (Figure 6). Protection therefore looks relatively inexpensive compared with history, although subdued pricing also suggests investors are not expecting a major policy surprise. Given the limited fiscal space and elevated gilt yields, this leaves scope for a larger GBP reaction if the Budget fails to convince investors on the sustainability of the fiscal path. While the UK’s fiscal position looks less precarious than its peers, Healey will need to tread carefully in his first Budget to avoid the same fate of his predecessors . Investors remain cautious, with limited gilt demand, persistent sterling outflows and heavy FX hedging. Yet options are pricing relatively muted moves , creating a disconnect between cautious positioning and subdued event pricing. We see the GBP vulnerable to a larger-than-priced move if the Budget substantially worsens the borrowing outlook, while a credible package that preserves fiscal discipline could support sterling given already bearish positioning. 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% Oct 25 Jan 26 Apr 26 Jul 26 Oct 26 20-day flow

records.text: Paul Gabard Filippo Ferone 20 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General UK Budget Preview : Time to Heal(ey) ? Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next week comes with little room for error. Fiscal space has likely eroded since March and gilt yields sit at the top of the G7 range, even though the UK's medium -term fiscal trajectory still compares favourably with its peers. Investors are clearly cautious: our flow data show limited gilt demand, persistent sterling outflows and hedging behaviour consistent with a bearish GBP view. Yet GBP options are pricing a rather quiet Budget Day. This disconnect between defensive positioning and cheap event pricing leaves sterling exposed to a larger -than- priced move if the Budget disappoints, while a credible package could support GBP given how pessimistic positioning already is. The OBR estimated in March that the Chancellor had around £24bn of headroom against the fiscal rules, an improvement on the relatively thin buffers available at several recent fiscal events (Figure 1). Part of that recovery reflected policy choices, includ ing welfare and spending reductions alongside tax increases, while a better borrowing outlook and stronger equity markets also helped. Even so, £2 3.6bn remains a modest cushion relative to the uncertainty surrounding the economic and fiscal forecasts. This divergence in rate -differentials and GBP flows is what prompts us to hold a net-bearish sterling view going into the Budget. Figure 5 Hedging points to GBP bearishness Source: State Street Markets Real money hedging activity ahead of the Budget is also very telling of the bearish sentiment towards sterling (Figure 5). Foreign investors continue to hedge their GBP exposure heavily, as they have for most of the year. Their hedge ratio now sits at roughly 45%, which is at the top of its historical range. Greater h edging on UK equities has accounted for most of the increase, with hedging on UK fixed income still holding around its 10-year median. The bigger shift, though, has come from UK -based investors. The domestic hedge ratio, which measures the share of overseas assets UK investors are hedging, has dropped sharply from 70% in June to 51%, its lowest since October 20 17. So, while there is hope that Healey can avoid the budget mishaps that the UK has become accustomed to, GBP investors, both foreign and domestic, certainly seem positioned for disappointment. 2 Insights Information Classification: General Our flow data suggests institutional investors are taking a less sanguine view on gilts, with net -selling across almost every segment of the curve (Figure 4). Yet outflows from the UK have been relatively measured, particularly compared with other European sovereign debt, which has borne the brunt of the recent shift into US Treasuries. Additionally, the picture across the gilt curve is more nuanced . At the short end, the initial bout in demand has quickly reversed, with little willingness to square existing underweights . By contrast, interest in the long end has proved more resilient, with demand for the 30 -year segment gradually improving since July. There it shows that investors remain reticent to trim their existing overweight. So, while it would be an overstatement to say gilt investors are positioned for disappointment, they are at least giving the UK government the benefit of the doubt.
